chunk_text: Good documentation practice requires records to be clear, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, complete, consistent, enduring and available. Corrections should preserve the original entry and include a reason, date and attributable signature where required.

A deviation is an unplanned departure from an approved instruction or established procedure. It should be documented promptly, assessed for impact, investigated to an appropriate depth and closed with justified actions.

Corrective action addresses the cause of a detected nonconformity to prevent recurrence. Preventive action addresses a potential nonconformity. Effectiveness checks should verify that actions achieved the intended outcome.

Proposed changes affecting validated processes, equipment, materials, software or controlled documents should be evaluated before implementation. The assessment should consider risk, validation, training, regulatory impact and approvals.
Data should be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, and also complete, consistent, enduring and available. Controls should protect records throughout their lifecycle.
Audit trails should capture who performed an action, what changed, when it occurred and, where appropriate, why. Audit-trail review should be risk-based and performed by authorized personnel.

Electronic records should be protected against unauthorized access, alteration, loss and deletion. Access should be role-based, and system controls should support record authenticity and traceability.

Electronic signatures should be attributable to an individual and linked to the relevant electronic record. Authentication and signature controls should be defined by the applicable system and regulatory requirements.
Personnel should be trained on procedures relevant to their assigned responsibilities before performing tasks independently. Training completion and assessment should be documented.
Equipment intended for regulated use should be appropriately qualified for its intended purpose. Qualification activities and acceptance criteria should be documented and approved.

Process validation provides documented evidence that a process can consistently produce output meeting predetermined requirements. The lifecycle approach includes process design, qualification and continued process verification.

Cleaning validation provides documented evidence that an approved cleaning process consistently reduces residues to predetermined acceptable levels. Sampling methods, limits and rationale should be scientifically justified.

An out-of-specification result is a result outside an established acceptance criterion. The result should be promptly documented and investigated under an approved procedure; it should not be invalidated without scientifically justified evidence.
An out-of-trend result may remain within specification but differ from the expected historical pattern. Trending and investigation can help identify emerging process or analytical issues.
Quality risk management should use a structured process to assess, control, communicate and review risks. The level of formality and documentation should be proportionate to the risk.
Suppliers of materials or services that can affect product quality should be evaluated and approved using a documented, risk-based process. Performance should be monitored periodically.
Controlled procedures should have an approved version, effective date, owner and defined review process. Obsolete versions should be prevented from unintended use.

Batch records should be reviewed for completeness, accuracy, deviations, reconciliation and required approvals before batch disposition. Missing or inconsistent entries should be resolved through approved processes.
Product complaints should be recorded, evaluated and investigated according to their potential impact. Relevant trends and reportability obligations should be assessed under applicable procedures.
A recall procedure should define responsibilities, escalation, traceability, communication and effectiveness checks. Mock recalls can test the ability to identify and reconcile affected product.
Computerized systems used in regulated activities should be fit for intended use. Validation should be risk-based and supported by requirements, testing, traceability and controlled change.
System access should be granted according to job responsibilities and least-privilege principles. Access rights should be approved, periodically reviewed and removed when no longer needed.
Critical electronic records should be backed up according to defined procedures. Restoration should be tested periodically, and backup integrity and retention should be monitored.
Laboratory procedures should define methods, equipment, reagents, calculations, acceptance criteria and review responsibilities. Records should allow reconstruction of the activity.
Analytical methods should be demonstrated suitable for their intended purpose. Relevant characteristics may include accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, range, detection limit and robustness.
Stability studies should use an approved protocol, defined storage conditions, time points and test methods. Results should be evaluated against predefined acceptance criteria.
Environmental monitoring programs should define locations, frequencies, methods, alert/action levels and response procedures. Excursions should be assessed and documented.
A nonconformance is a failure to meet a specified requirement. It should be identified, contained where appropriate, documented and evaluated for product and quality-system impact.
Regulatory submission information should be accurate, internally consistent, traceable to approved source records and maintained under document-control procedures.

Management review should evaluate the continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the quality management system using relevant performance data, audit outcomes, complaints, CAPA and improvement opportunities.
